h1: How Much Does a Lobby Sign Cost in NYC?
author: Vision Graphics New York
lead_html:
Most lobby signs in NYC cost roughly $500 to $10,000 for the sign itself. Acrylic sits at the low end, brushed metal and dimensional letters in the mid-to-high range, and lit signs above that. Installation, removal, wall patching, and building requirements in New York are priced separately.

This guide breaks down lobby sign cost in NYC by material, then covers the building costs that general price guides leave out. See our lobby signs in NYC for the sign types themselves.

sections.html:
These are planning ranges for the sign alone, based on published prices from sign companies in New York and elsewhere. Your quote will differ. Installation is priced separately and commonly adds a few hundred dollars to a couple of thousand, depending on the wall, the height, and the building.

MaterialLookTypical price range (sign only)Lead time
AcrylicGlossy, vivid color, takes backlighting$500 to $3,5002 to 3 weeks
Painted aluminumSmooth, solid color in a chosen finish$1,000 to $4,0002 to 4 weeks
Brushed metalTextured metallic grain with a refined look$2,000 to $10,0002 to 4 weeks
Dimensional lettersRaised letters with depth and shadow$1,500 to $7,5002 to 4 weeks
Lit signs (halo-lit or backlit)Glowing letters or a lit panel$2,000 to $8,000+3 to 5 weeks, plus electrical and approval time

The cost of dimensional letters depends on the material they are cut from, so that row overlaps the others. It shows the price of a letter-cut logo. Small plaques can be priced below these ranges.

Two lobby signs that look alike can cost different amounts. Seven things drive the gap. You can see the full range on our interior signs page.

Size

Bigger signs cost more. Area drives material and labor, and a wide reception wall takes more letters or a larger panel.

Number and Depth of Letters

More letters mean more cutting and finishing. Deeper letters add material and weight, so mounting takes longer too.

Finish

Painted, brushed, and polished finishes cost different amounts. Mixing finishes on one sign adds steps.

Lighting

Lit signs add LEDs, power supplies, and electrical work. A licensed electrician makes the final connection; in-wall wiring can change the scope.

Mounting Method

Standoffs, adhesive, and rail systems each need different hardware and wall prep. A heavy sign needs a more secure mount than a light panel.

Wall Condition

Tile, stone, glass, and older drywall change how a sign attaches, and a wall in poor shape may need repairs first. Wall condition and access also shape the scope, so we ask early about drilling and adhesive limits.

Artwork Complexity

A simple wordmark costs less to cut than a detailed logo with fine lines, small openings, or several colors.

In New York, the sign is only part of the bill. Each cost below depends on your building, so treat these as items to ask about. None of them is a fixed fee.

After-Hours Installation

Many NYC buildings allow signage work only outside business hours. Evening and weekend installs can add labor charges, and some buildings pass on their own staffing costs. Ask your property manager for the building's fee schedule, and tell us your hours so we can price it into your quote. See how we handle sign installation in NYC.

Certificate of Insurance

[[image:nyc-lobby-sign-cost-nyc-certificate-of-insurance-01]]

Most NYC buildings require a certificate of insurance before a vendor works on site. Buildings set their own coverage wording and limits, and a certificate alone does not add anyone as an additional insured. We provide a certificate on request, and sending your building's requirements early helps avoid delays on install day.

Building Management Approval

Interior signs usually need approval from building management or the landlord before work starts. Approval may require drawings, mounting details, and installer insurance, and high-rise buildings in Manhattan can take longer to review. Ask if your building charges for review.

Booking the Freight Elevator or Loading Dock

Freight elevators and loading docks have limited windows, so you must book deliveries ahead. If a sign arrives outside its slot, the install can slip by days. Some buildings also charge for freight elevator time. Tell us your dock hours and elevator rules, and we plan delivery and the crew around them.

Removal and Disposal of the Old Sign

Taking down the old sign is its own line item. New York City requires a licensed sign hanger for most removals, and disposal and wall repair add to the scope. We plan removal alongside the new install so the changeover is quick. Our sign installation in NYC page explains the full process.

Wall Patching and Paint

[[image:nyc-lobby-sign-cost-nyc-wall-patching-and-paint-01]]

Old signs leave holes, marks, and adhesive behind. Your quote includes patching and paint touch-ups based on wall photos, and repainting a full wall costs more than touching up a few spots. Check what your lease requires when a sign comes down, and send wall photos with your quote request.

sections.h2: Example: Replacing a Lobby, Reception and Elevator Sign
sections.html:
An office manager in New York asked for three signs: a logo with mounted words behind the reception desk, a smaller sign at the desk, and a plaque at the elevator lobby. The old signs had to come down, and the walls had to be patched. Reception area signage in NYC usually mixes a main lobby sign with smaller signs, so this example prices all three together.

It is an illustrative planning example. It is not a quote.

ItemAcrylicPainted aluminumBrushed metal
Lobby logo with mounted words$1,500 to $3,500$2,000 to $4,000$3,000 to $7,500
Reception sign$500 to $1,200$800 to $1,800$1,200 to $3,000
Elevator-lobby plaque$300 to $800$400 to $1,000$500 to $1,500
Signs subtotal$2,300 to $5,500$3,200 to $6,800$4,700 to $12,000

The reception sign cost sits between the lobby logo and the plaque in all three materials. Not in these totals: removal and wall patching (scoped in your quote), installation (set by the wall, the height, and the building), and after-hours and building costs (set by your building).

In an example like this, the material choice moves the sign subtotal by several thousand dollars, while removal, patching, and building costs tend to stay similar across all three. The elevator-lobby plaque here is a wayfinding or decorative sign, and building-code signs are handled separately.

Most lobby signs take two to five weeks from approved drawing to installation. Acrylic runs about two to three weeks, dimensional and metal signs two to four, and lit signs three to five, plus electrical and approval time.

Most of our signs are made in Salt Lake City and shipped, so transit time is added and confirmed in your quote. Building approval, freight elevator booking, and after-hours scheduling can add days, so ask for your building's rules before you set a date.

sections.h2: How to Get an Accurate Quote
sections.html:
You can get a first price from photos and rough sizes. Send these four things:

  • Photos: the wall, the old sign, and a wide shot of the lobby.
  • Dimensions: the wall width, the sign width you want, and the height from the floor.
  • Artwork: your logo files, ideally vector files such as AI, EPS, or PDF.
  • Building rules: insurance requirements, work hours, drilling and adhesive limits, and dock or elevator rules.

The same list works for office signs and other interior signs, where office sign cost follows the same drivers.

Vision Graphics quotes show the sign, installation, removal, and wall patching as separate lines, with material options side by side, so you can see which choice moves the price. If a building fee is still unknown, the quote says so, and we update it once your property manager confirms the amount.

We can price the sign and installation based on photos and sizes. Building fees such as overtime, freight elevator, or review charges come from your building, so ask your property manager for the fee schedule. Request a quote, and we will go through the rest with you.

items.a_html: Usually yes. Acrylic sign cost typically runs below brushed metal at the same size, and acrylic takes color and backlighting well. Metal costs more and wears better in busy lobbies. The gap depends on size, finish, and lighting, so compare both on your wall before you decide.

Removal is part of our install plan, and it appears as its own line in your quote. The old sign comes down before the new one goes up. Wall patching and paint touch-up are scoped separately, based on photos of your wall.

Usually yes. Building management or the landlord typically approves interior signs before work starts, and many buildings ask for drawings, mounting details, and an installer's certificate of insurance. Ask your property manager early, and we will prepare the drawings they need.

items.q: Can the sign be installed after hours?
items.a_html: Yes. We schedule installs around your building's rules, including evenings, weekends, and freight elevator windows. After-hours work can add labor charges, and we confirm them in your quote. Tell us your building's work hours and dock rules when you request a quote.

items.q: How long does a lobby sign last?
items.a_html: An indoor lobby sign usually lasts many years. Metal tends to wear best in busy areas, and acrylic can scratch and may yellow under long direct sun. Gentle cleaning and keeping the sign out of harsh direct light help it last longer.

items.q: Is installation included in these prices?
items.a_html: No. The ranges in this guide are for the sign itself. Installation is priced separately and depends on the wall, the sign's weight and height, and your building's rules. We show installation as its own line in your quote so you can compare it.
